catholic.abortion:
The Catholic Church teaches that human life begins at conception and is to be protected from that moment, so that deliberately ending an unborn child's life is a grave moral wrong. The Church holds that this applies to every stage, and it attaches a canonical penalty, excommunication, to those who procure a completed abortion.

Catholics distinguish direct abortion from medical treatment that has the death of the unborn child as an unintended side effect, such as treating a life-threatening illness in the mother. The Church also stresses practical and pastoral help for women in difficult pregnancies, and forgiveness through the sacrament of Reconciliation. Many Protestants share the conviction about the unborn, while Protestant denominations differ among themselves, so the Catholic position is more uniform and more formally stated.
evangelical.abortion:
Most Evangelicals hold that human life is sacred from conception because human beings are made in the image of God, and they often cite passages such as Psalm 139 about God's care for a person before birth. On this basis Evangelicals generally oppose abortion, and many take part in pro-life advocacy, in pregnancy care centers, and in adoption and foster care ministries.

Evangelicals are not unanimous about every case. Some allow exceptions for the life of the mother or for pregnancies resulting from rape, while others hold that no exception should be made. Their stance is stronger and more consistent than in many mainline Protestant denominations, some of which have issued statements that allow for more choice, so a Protestant reader may find the Evangelical position sits at the firmer end of the Protestant range.
ortho.abortion:
The Eastern Orthodox Church regards abortion as the taking of human life and as a serious sin, and it has held this view from the early centuries. Orthodox teaching understands life to be a gift from God that begins at conception and is to be protected.

Orthodox practice is pastoral as well as firm. A person who has had or been involved in an abortion is called to repentance and can be forgiven and restored through confession, guided by a spiritual father, and hard cases such as a threat to the mother's life are handled with pastoral discernment rather than by a single legal rule. Unlike the Catholic Church, Orthodoxy has no single central body that issues a detailed, unified code, so statements come from the various national churches and their bishops.
adventist.alcohol:
Adventists teach abstinence from alcohol. They understand the body to be the temple of the Holy Spirit, and hold that Christians are responsible for caring for their health. Abstaining from alcohol, tobacco and other harmful substances is part of what Adventists call the health message, and it is commonly part of the commitment made by those who join the church.

Many Adventists also read the references to wine in the Bible as sometimes meaning unfermented grape juice, while recognizing that fermented wine is also mentioned and warned against. For a Protestant reader whose tradition permits moderate drinking, the difference is that Adventists do not treat moderation as the aim. They understand abstinence to be a witness and a way of honoring God in daily life. It is presented as a matter of conviction and health, not as a way of earning salvation.
catholic.alcohol:
Catholics regard alcohol as a good gift of God to be used with temperance, which is one of the moral virtues. Wine is central to the Mass, and drinking in moderation at meals and celebrations is accepted throughout Catholic life. Drunkenness, however, is sinful, especially when it destroys a person's reason and self-control or harms others.

Some Catholics choose to abstain altogether, for reasons of health or discipline, or out of concern for those struggling with addiction, and they may see it as a form of penance or sacrifice. The Church does not require abstinence as a rule of Catholic life. A Protestant reader who comes from a tradition of total abstinence will find that Catholics generally treat the question as one of moderation, and not as a mark of holiness in itself.
holiness.alcohol:
Holiness churches ask their members to practice total abstinence from alcohol, and often from tobacco and similar things as well. This comes from the Wesleyan-Holiness emphasis on entire sanctification: the expectation that a life set apart for God will show itself in practical self-denial and in care for the body as the temple of the Spirit.

There is also a strong heritage of temperance in these churches, which grew up alongside the movement against the harm alcohol was doing in families and communities. Many Protestant traditions leave drinking to Christian freedom or moderation, so a Protestant reader will notice that Holiness churches treat abstinence as something closer to a shared commitment of members. It is meant to be held out of love for God and not as a means of salvation, though in some churches it is a condition of membership.
lds.alcohol:
Latter-day Saints follow the Word of Wisdom, a health code found in the Doctrine and Covenants, one of their books of scripture. They understand it to have been given by revelation in the 1830s, and it teaches abstaining from alcoholic drinks, tobacco, and hot drinks, which is understood to mean tea and coffee, while encouraging healthy foods.

Latter-day Saints treat this as a commandment with spiritual blessings attached, and keeping it is a requirement for entering their temples. The sacrament in their services uses water and not wine. Many Protestant traditions permit moderate drinking or leave it to conscience, and even those that prefer abstinence do not usually base it on a book of scripture that Protestants do not accept. For Latter-day Saints, the Word of Wisdom is part of a broader teaching on caring for the body as a gift from God.
baptist.altar_call:
In many Baptist churches, the sermon ends with an invitation: a time, often accompanied by a hymn such as Just As I Am, when people are invited to come forward to the front of the church. Those who come may be professing faith in Christ for the first time, asking for baptism or church membership, or seeking prayer and rededication.

Baptists understand this as a way of making a public response to the message, in line with their emphasis on a personal profession of faith. It is not required for salvation, and practice varies. Some Baptist churches use it every Sunday, and others rarely or not at all. A Protestant reader from a church without an altar call, such as a Lutheran or Reformed congregation, may find it helpful to know that Baptists see it as an opportunity to respond, not as a sacrament or a rite.
evangelical.altar_call:
In many Evangelical churches the service ends with an altar call: an invitation for people to come forward, or to raise a hand or pray, to receive Christ or to make a new commitment. It grew out of the revivalist preaching of earlier centuries, in which hearers were urged to make a decision for Christ.

Counselors or pastors often meet those who come forward, and the moment is meant to give a concrete way to respond. Evangelicals hold that salvation comes through faith, so the altar call is not seen as a rite that saves in itself. Practice varies, and some Evangelical churches, especially those that lean Reformed, are cautious about it because they worry it may suggest that a walk to the front produces conversion. Many Protestant traditions have no such practice.
pentecostal.altar_call:
In Pentecostal churches the altar is the front area of the sanctuary, and an altar call is an invitation to come forward to pray. It is used for a wider range of needs than a decision for Christ. People may come to be saved, to be healed, to be filled with the Holy Spirit, or simply to seek God in prayer.

Often the altar time is unhurried, with the congregation praying and worship music continuing, and members may gather around those who come forward to pray with them. Pentecostals use the word altar for a place of prayer and surrender, not of sacrifice. A Protestant reader familiar with a short invitation at the end of a sermon should expect that in Pentecostal worship the altar time can be a central and lengthy part of the service.
adventist.annihilation:
Adventists teach conditional immortality: human beings are not naturally immortal, and only God grants immortality, as a gift to the saved through Christ. It follows that the wicked will not live forever in torment, and that after the final judgment they will be destroyed, and will cease to exist.

Adventists read biblical language about eternal fire as fire whose result is permanent, and not as a burning that never ends. They see this as more consistent with God's justice and love, and they emphasize that it is an act of God's judgment against sin. This differs from the view of eternal conscious torment held by many Protestants, though some Protestant writers, including some Evangelical scholars, also hold to conditional immortality. Adventists distinguish it from universalism, since they teach that the lost are lost.
catholic.annihilation:
The Catholic Church teaches that hell is real and eternal: those who die in a state of mortal sin, having freely and finally rejected God, remain separated from him forever. Catholic teaching describes the chief punishment of hell as this eternal separation from God, for whom human beings were made.

The Church teaches that the soul is immortal, so it does not accept that the lost simply cease to exist. It has never declared that any particular person is in hell, and it encourages hope and prayer for the salvation of all. The word punishment in Catholic teaching is not mainly about torture, and the Church has not settled the details of its nature. A Protestant reader who knows the phrase eternal conscious torment will find that Catholic teaching emphasizes separation from God.
jehovahs_witnesses.annihilation:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the wicked who persist in rejecting God will be destroyed forever, and not tormented. They read the biblical words for everlasting punishment and destruction as meaning that the person ceases to exist, with no hope of a future resurrection.

They base this on their teaching that human beings do not have an immortal soul: the soul is the person, and when the person dies, the person is gone. This judgment is expected to come at Armageddon and at the end of Christ's thousand-year rule. Some Protestants also believe in the final destruction of the lost, called conditional immortality, but Witnesses reach it through their own teaching about God, Christ and the soul, which differs from Protestant teaching in other ways.
ortho.annihilation:
Eastern Orthodox teaching affirms that the finally impenitent are in eternal punishment, but it understands this differently from much Protestant teaching. Many Orthodox writers describe hell not as a place where God tortures the lost, but as the experience of God's own love and presence by those who have refused to love him. The same divine light which brings joy to the saved becomes torment to those who resist it.

This is not an official definition, and Orthodox writers have used varied images. The Church does not teach that the soul ceases to exist, and it does not teach purgatory. Some Orthodox theologians hope that all may finally be saved, while holding that this cannot be taught as a doctrine. A Protestant reader will notice that the emphasis falls on the state of the person's heart in relation to God, and less on a legal sentence.
catholic.anointing_of_the_sick:
In the Anointing of the Sick, a Catholic priest anoints the forehead and hands of a person who is seriously ill, elderly or about to undergo major surgery, with oil blessed by the bishop, and prays for them. Catholics base this on the passage in the Letter of James, where the elders are called to anoint the sick with oil and pray.

It is one of the seven sacraments, and Catholics believe it gives strength, peace and courage, forgiveness of sins where needed, and sometimes physical healing, according to God's will. It was formerly known as Extreme Unction and associated mainly with the dying, but it is now understood as for anyone seriously ill, and may be received more than once. A Protestant reader may know the practice of anointing from James, but the Catholic understanding treats it as a sacrament administered by a priest.
ortho.anointing_of_the_sick:
The Eastern Orthodox Church celebrates Holy Unction, one of its Holy Mysteries, in which a priest anoints a sick person with blessed oil and prays for the healing of soul and body. It is based on the teaching in the Letter of James about anointing the sick with oil.

Holy Unction is not reserved for the dying, and is offered to anyone who is ill. In many places a communal service of Holy Unction is held during Holy Week, in which all the faithful may be anointed for healing and forgiveness, whether or not they are sick. Orthodox teaching links the healing of the body with the forgiveness of sins and the restoration of the whole person. A Protestant reader may be familiar with anointing from the New Testament, but should note that the Orthodox understand it as a sacramental act performed by the clergy.
pentecostal.anointing_of_the_sick:
Pentecostals anoint the sick with oil and pray for healing, following the instruction in the Letter of James that a sick person should call for the elders, who anoint with oil and pray in faith. The oil is a symbol of the Holy Spirit and is not thought to have power of its own.

Pentecostals expect that God heals today, and prayer for the sick is a regular part of worship, often with the laying on of hands. They recognize that not everyone is healed in the way or at the time they desire, and most also make use of doctors. Many other Protestants also pray for the sick and some anoint with oil, but Pentecostals put greater weight on healing as a present sign of the gospel, and on expecting God to act in the meeting.
anglican.apocrypha:
Anglicans include the Apocrypha in the Bible and read passages from it in worship, but do not use it to establish doctrine. Article Six of the Thirty-Nine Articles states that the church reads these books for example of life and instruction of manners, but does not apply them to establish any doctrine.

This places Anglicans between the Catholic and Orthodox churches, which treat these books as fully Scripture, and Protestant traditions that omit them from their Bibles altogether. Many Protestant Bibles since the nineteenth century have not printed these books, though the earliest Protestant Bibles, including the King James Version as first published, did include them. An Anglican lectionary regularly includes readings from these books, so Anglicans hear them in church even where they are not printed in the pew Bible.
catholic.apocrypha:
Catholics hold that the Old Testament includes several books that Protestants often call the Apocrypha, and which Catholics call the deuterocanonical books. They include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the two books of Maccabees, along with additions to Esther and Daniel. Catholics accept these as inspired Scripture, and the Council of Trent affirmed their place in the canon.

The Catholic Old Testament therefore has forty-six books, compared with the thirty-nine in most Protestant Bibles, which follow the Hebrew Scriptures. Catholics note that the early Christian church commonly used the Greek translation of the Old Testament which contained these books. They do not use the word Apocrypha for them, since Catholics apply that word to other ancient writings which are not accepted as Scripture. The difference is one of the clearest between Catholic and Protestant Bibles.
ortho.apocrypha:
The Eastern Orthodox Church receives the books which Protestants call the Apocrypha as part of the Old Testament, following the Greek Septuagint, which was the Bible of the early church. The Orthodox often call them the anagignoskomena, a Greek word meaning things worthy to be read, and they are read in the church's worship.

The Orthodox Old Testament is somewhat larger than the Catholic, and includes additional books such as Third Maccabees and Psalm 151, and the exact list differs slightly among Orthodox churches. Some Orthodox writers distinguish these books from the others as a second rank, but the Church does not treat them as a lesser or optional section of the Bible. A Protestant reader whose Bible omits these books will find that Orthodox Christians hear them as part of Scripture in worship.
lds.apostles_today:
Latter-day Saints believe that Christ has apostles in his church today, as he did in the New Testament. The church is led by the First Presidency and the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, who are called and ordained and are regarded as special witnesses of Christ throughout the world. The senior apostle serves as the president of the church and is sustained as prophet, seer and revelator.

Latter-day Saints understand the apostolic office to have been lost after the first century and restored through Joseph Smith in the nineteenth century. They believe that these apostles receive revelation for the church as a whole. Many Protestants hold that the apostolic age ended with the first generation, so a Protestant reader will recognize the word apostle but should note that the office is understood as continuing.
new_apostolic.apostles_today:
The New Apostolic Church believes that Christ still calls and sends apostles, the same office found in the New Testament, and that this continuing apostleship is how he guides his church today. The apostles preach the gospel, announce the forgiveness of sins, administer the sacraments, and ordain ministers. The church is led by a Chief Apostle, with other apostles serving as his co-workers.

Members do not regard the apostles as adding books to Scripture. The Bible remains the foundation, and the apostles are understood as interpreting and applying it, and as caring for the unity of the church. A Protestant reader who holds that the apostolic age ended in the first century will find that the New Apostolic Church regards the office as continuing, and that it treats a sacrament called Holy Sealing, given through an apostle, as conveying the gift of the Holy Spirit.
pentecostal.apostles_today:
Some Pentecostal and charismatic groups believe that God still calls apostles today, and they cite the list in the Letter to the Ephesians of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, often called the fivefold ministry. In practice, a modern apostle is usually someone who plants churches or oversees a network of churches, and not someone who holds authority equal to that of the original Twelve.

Not all Pentecostals use the title. Many of the historic Pentecostal denominations do not recognize apostles in this sense, and use the word mainly to describe the first apostles or to mean missionary. Those who do recognize apostles generally hold that their teaching must be tested by Scripture and that they are accountable to other leaders. A Protestant reader who holds that the apostolic age is over will find this a point on which Pentecostals differ among themselves as well.
anglican.apostolic_succession:
Anglicans have kept the historic episcopate, which means that their bishops are consecrated by the laying on of hands in a line reaching back to the apostles. It is one of four features named in the Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral, along with Scripture, the creeds and the two sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

Anglicans do not all understand it the same way. Anglo-Catholics regard it as essential to a valid ministry and sacraments. Many Evangelical Anglicans value it as a sign of the church's continuity and unity but do not treat it as necessary for a church to be a true church. Anglicans have generally not denied that other Protestant churches have real ministries. A Protestant reader from a church without bishops should note that Anglicans hold the office to be historic and useful, and, for many, not something that invalidates other churches.
catholic.apostolic_succession:
The Catholic Church teaches that the bishops are the successors of the apostles, in an unbroken line of ordination by the laying on of hands reaching back to the apostles themselves. The Bishop of Rome, the pope, is understood to be the successor of the apostle Peter. This succession is understood to guarantee the continuity of the apostolic teaching and of valid sacraments, especially the Eucharist and ordination.

Catholics do not deny that Protestants have genuine faith in Christ and the gift of Baptism, but they teach that churches without this succession of ordination lack the sacramental priesthood in the full sense. Most Protestants understand apostolic succession as a matter of teaching, meaning faithfulness to what the apostles taught, and not of a line of ordinations. Catholics hold that both belong together.
lds.apostolic_succession:
Latter-day Saints do not teach an unbroken chain of authority from the apostles to the present. They hold that the authority of the priesthood was lost in what they call the Great Apostasy, after the first century, and restored in the 1820s and 1830s. In their account, Peter, James and John and John the Baptist appeared as heavenly messengers and conferred priesthood authority on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery.

From that restoration, they believe, a line of authority runs through the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. The senior apostle becomes the president of the church when the president dies. So Latter-day Saints do teach a succession, but one that began with the restoration and not one that continued unbroken from the first century. A Protestant reader should note the word succession is used here for a different pattern from that of the Catholic or Anglican view.
oriental_ortho.apostolic_succession:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, hold that their bishops stand in apostolic succession, continuing through the laying on of hands from the apostles. Each of these churches traces its own history to an apostle or apostolic figure, such as the tradition that Mark founded the church in Alexandria.

The succession is understood as more than a chain of ordinations. It expresses the continuity of the apostles' faith and sacramental life within the church, in which the bishop is the center of the local community. Because these churches hold a distinct teaching about the person of Christ, they have been separate from other churches since the fifth century, but they hold the same view of the apostolic office. A Protestant reader will find the idea of a continuous, historical line important to their self-understanding.
ortho.apostolic_succession:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that its bishops stand in apostolic succession, in an unbroken line of ordination going back to the apostles. It is understood as more than a chain of hands. It expresses that the church has kept the apostles' faith and sacramental life continuously, and the bishop is the center of unity of his local church.

Orthodoxy does not teach that one bishop, such as the Bishop of Rome, holds a universal authority as the successor of Peter. All bishops are considered to share the same apostolic ministry, and they come together in councils to settle questions of faith. A Protestant reader who understands apostolic succession as faithfulness to apostolic teaching will find that the Orthodox hold both together: a historical line of ordination and a living continuity in the faith.
catholic.ascension:
Catholics celebrate the Ascension of Christ forty days after Easter, often on a Thursday, though in many countries the feast is moved to the following Sunday. They believe that Jesus, after his resurrection, was taken up bodily into heaven, as recorded in the Gospels and in the Acts of the Apostles, and that he sits at the right hand of the Father.

Catholics understand the Ascension as the completion of his earthly work and the beginning of his heavenly intercession for the church. They also connect it with the promise of the Holy Spirit and of his return. It is confessed in the Creed. A Protestant reader will find the Catholic belief in the event the same. The difference lies in its place in the church's liturgical year and in the way Catholics connect Christ's heavenly priesthood with the Mass.
lds.ascension:
Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus rose bodily from the dead and ascended into heaven, as described in the Acts of the Apostles. They understand his resurrected body to be a glorified body of flesh and bone, and they believe that he continues to live and serve as the head of his church.

The Book of Mormon, a scripture accepted by Latter-day Saints, tells of Christ appearing to people in the Americas after his resurrection, and Latter-day Saints hold that this was part of his ministry after rising. They also teach that he will come again. A Protestant reader will find that the basic belief in the Ascension is shared, while noting that Latter-day Saints understand it as part of a longer post-resurrection ministry which Protestant Christians do not accept.
ortho.ascension:
The Eastern Orthodox Church celebrates the Ascension as one of the twelve Great Feasts of the church year, forty days after Pascha, the Orthodox name for Easter. It teaches that Christ ascended in his body, and that in doing so he carried human nature into the presence of God.

For the Orthodox, this is not only the departure of Jesus but an event of great significance for human beings: in Christ, humanity is raised to the throne of God. It is linked to the Orthodox teaching that human beings are called to share in the divine life. The feast looks forward to Pentecost and to the return of Christ. A Protestant reader will recognize the biblical event, and find that Orthodox worship gives it great weight as a celebration of humanity's exaltation.
catholic.assumption:
Catholics believe in the Assumption of Mary: that at the end of her earthly life the Virgin Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory. This was declared a dogma of the Catholic Church in 1950, and the church celebrates it on August 15.

The Bible does not describe the event. Catholics rely on the ancient tradition of the church, which spoke of it from early centuries, and on the belief that Mary, who bore the Lord and shared uniquely in his work, has already received the resurrection promised to all the faithful. The definition does not say whether Mary died first. Many Protestants do not accept the teaching because it is not found in Scripture, and Catholics acknowledge that it rests on tradition and on the church's teaching authority.
oriental_ortho.assumption:
The Oriental Orthodox churches keep a feast of the Dormition, or falling asleep, of the Virgin Mary, in which they celebrate her death and her being taken up to be with Christ. It is observed in the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and other Oriental Orthodox churches, often in August, and with considerable devotion.

These churches have kept the tradition in their liturgy and hymns, and honor Mary as the Mother of God. It is not defined in a formal dogmatic statement, and it is received as part of the church's living tradition rather than as an article proved from Scripture. A Protestant reader, who will find no account of Mary's end in the Bible, should note that this belief is held on the authority of the church's ancient worship and teaching.
ortho.assumption:
The Eastern Orthodox Church celebrates the Dormition of the Mother of God, the falling asleep of Mary, on August 15, by the calendar the church uses. It teaches that Mary died a natural death, like all people, and that Christ then received her soul and raised her and took her, body and soul, to be with him in heaven.

The well-known icon of the Dormition shows Christ standing over her, holding her soul as a small child. The Orthodox do not define this as a dogma by a council, but it has been the church's shared faith and worship since early centuries. The Orthodox hold it as a sign of the promise of resurrection. A Protestant reader will notice that the belief rests on tradition, which the Orthodox regard as living and authoritative alongside Scripture.
catholic.assurance:
Catholics are taught to have a firm hope of salvation, based on God's promises, on Christ's work, and on the sacraments. They do not, however, teach that a person can have absolute certainty of their own final salvation, unless God gives a special revelation, because they hold that each person must persevere and that grace can be lost through grave sin.

This is meant to keep hope honest. It is not intended to leave people anxious. The Church also warns against despair, and against presumption, that is, taking salvation for granted. Regular confession and the Eucharist are understood as ways of keeping in God's grace. A Protestant reader from a tradition that stresses knowing that one is saved should note that Catholics use the language of hope and confidence rather than certainty, and that they speak of salvation as a process that continues through life.
evangelical.assurance:
Evangelicals commonly teach that a believer can know that he or she is saved, and can have assurance of salvation now. They base this on the promises of Scripture, such as the statement in the First Letter of John that it was written so believers may know they have eternal life, and on the inner witness of the Holy Spirit and the fruit of a changed life.

Many Evangelicals hold that those who trust in Christ cannot lose their salvation, while others in the Wesleyan tradition teach that assurance is real but that a person may fall away. Pastors often encourage doubting believers to look to Christ and to his promises, and to the evidence of God's work in their lives. The phrase knowing you are saved is sometimes used by outsiders as a shorthand for this emphasis, and Evangelicals themselves speak of assurance as a gift of God.
ortho.assurance:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not usually speak of assurance of salvation in the way many Protestants do. Orthodox Christians trust in God's mercy and love and strive to live in repentance and prayer, but they generally avoid saying that they are certain of their own salvation, because they understand salvation as a lifelong journey of growth into union with God.

Humility is prized, and it is considered dangerous to think of oneself as finished or secure. Yet the Orthodox are not anxious, and place hope in Christ and in his church. A Protestant reader will notice that the question is framed differently. The Orthodox look less at a moment when one is saved and more at a continuing process of being saved, and would say that hope in God's mercy, rather than a claim to certainty, is the right attitude.
reformed.assurance:
Reformed Christians teach that believers can be assured of their salvation. Assurance rests first on the promises of God in the gospel, then on the inward witness of the Holy Spirit, and also on the evidence of a changed life. It is understood as a gift, and Christians are encouraged to seek it.

The Westminster Confession adds that assurance is not part of the essence of faith, so a true believer may wait a long time to receive it, and may lose it for a time through sin or trial without ceasing to be saved. This is linked to the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints, that God will keep those he has chosen. Reformed pastors urge doubting believers to look to Christ and to his promises rather than to their feelings. Many Protestants share this emphasis, but Reformed teaching grounds it in God's election and preservation.
catholic.atonement:
Catholics teach that Christ's suffering and death on the cross was a sacrifice which redeemed humanity and reconciled it to God. A traditional way of explaining this is satisfaction: out of love, Jesus offered to the Father something greater than all the offense of sin, and so made amends on behalf of all people.

The Catholic Church has not defined a single theory of how the atonement works, and Catholic writers use several images: sacrifice, ransom, victory over sin and death, and healing. Christ's saving work is made present in the Mass and applied through the sacraments, and believers are invited to unite their own sufferings to his. A Protestant reader familiar with penal substitution should note that Catholic teaching also stresses Christ's sacrifice for sin, but usually places more weight on his love and on the restoration of the person.
christian_science.atonement:
In Christian Science, atonement is understood as at-one-ment, meaning the unity of God and humanity as shown by Christ Jesus. It is not the payment of a penalty or the placing of human guilt on Jesus. Christian Scientists teach that Jesus' life, teaching, suffering and resurrection showed that human beings are not really separated from God, and that sin, sickness and death can be overcome.

The cross is honored as a great proof of that unity, and Jesus' sacrifice is seen as real and costly. Salvation comes as each person understands and follows the truth that Jesus demonstrated. A Protestant reader who thinks of the atonement as Christ bearing sin's punishment in our place will find that Christian Science uses the same word for a different idea, and that it describes salvation as awakening to a unity that already exists.
lds.atonement:
Latter-day Saints speak of the Atonement of Jesus Christ as the center of their faith. They teach that it includes his suffering in the Garden of Gethsemane, his death on the cross and his resurrection. In Gethsemane, they believe, he took upon himself the sins, pains and sorrows of all people.

The Atonement, they believe, overcomes physical death for everyone, through the resurrection, and makes forgiveness of sins possible for those who have faith, repent, are baptized and keep their covenants. They teach that his grace makes up for what people cannot do themselves. A Protestant reader whose tradition places the main weight on the cross should note that Latter-day Saints give great emphasis to Gethsemane as well, and that their account of salvation includes ongoing obedience to commandments alongside grace.
ortho.atonement:
Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of redemption through Christ using many images from the early church. One of the most prominent is Christ's victory over death and the devil, sometimes called Christus Victor, in which he enters death and destroys its power by his resurrection. Others include ransom, sacrifice and the healing of human nature.

Orthodox teaching does not usually explain the cross as Christ receiving the punishment which God's justice demands, which is the emphasis of penal substitution in many Protestant churches. It understands sin more as a sickness and a bondage than a legal debt, and Christ as the physician and liberator. The cross and the resurrection are inseparable, and the purpose is union with God, or theosis. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox affirm that Christ died for our sins, but that they explain it in less legal terms.
reformed.atonement:
Reformed Christians teach that Christ's death was a penal substitution: on the cross he bore in our place the penalty that sin deserves, satisfying God's justice so that sinners can be forgiven. This is the most common way of explaining the atonement in Protestant churches, and Reformed teaching gives it a central place.

Many Reformed churches also teach limited atonement, also called particular redemption: Christ's death is sufficient for all, but was intended to secure the salvation of those whom the Father has chosen, and it accomplishes exactly what it was meant to do. This was set out at the Synod of Dort. Protestants in the Wesleyan or Arminian traditions hold that Christ died for all in the same sense and that all may respond. Some Reformed Christians prefer to stress the universal offer of the gospel alongside the particular purpose of the cross.
baptist.baptism:
Baptists practice believer's baptism: baptism by immersion, given only to those who are old enough to make a personal profession of faith in Christ. They understand it as an ordinance of obedience, and as a public sign of what has already happened in the believer, who is united with Christ in his death, burial and resurrection.

For most Baptists baptism does not save or convey grace by itself. It follows conversion, and it is usually the step by which a person joins a local church. They do not consider infant baptism to be baptism in the biblical sense, since an infant cannot believe. Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist Protestants baptize infants, so a Protestant reader from one of those churches will find that Baptists and they share a high view of Scripture but differ about who should be baptized and what baptism does.
catholic.baptism:
Catholics teach that Baptism is a sacrament in which a person is washed with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. It forgives original sin and any personal sins, gives new life in Christ, and makes the person a member of the Church.

Catholics baptize infants, holding that grace is a gift that does not depend on the child's understanding, and that the faith of parents and the Church supports the child. Baptism is received once and is not repeated. Catholics recognize as valid the baptisms of most Protestant churches which use water and the Trinitarian formula. A Protestant reader will note that Catholics see baptism as truly effective, not merely a sign, and see it as the door to the other sacraments.
churches_of_christ.baptism:
Churches of Christ teach that baptism is the immersion of a believer in water for the forgiveness of sins, drawing especially on the passage in Acts in which Peter tells the crowd to repent and be baptized. Together with faith, repentance and confession of Christ, it is understood as part of how a person responds to the gospel.

Members stress that the water has no power of its own and that it is God who forgives when a person is baptized in faith. It is not regarded as a human work that earns salvation. Baptists and many other Protestants agree with them that baptism should be by immersion and given to believers, but they usually teach that baptism follows salvation and symbolizes it. A Protestant reader should therefore note that Churches of Christ place the moment of forgiveness at baptism.
lds.baptism:
Latter-day Saints teach that baptism by immersion is necessary for salvation and for membership in the church. It is given at age eight or later, when a child is considered accountable, and after a person has faith in Christ and repents. It is performed by a member of the priesthood who has authority to do so, and is followed by the laying on of hands to confer the gift of the Holy Ghost.

They understand baptism as a covenant to follow Christ and as the means of forgiveness of sins. Because they hold that authority to baptize was restored through Joseph Smith, a person baptized in another church is baptized again on joining. They also teach that baptisms can be performed in temples on behalf of the dead. A Protestant reader will recognize the practice of immersion, but should note that Latter-day Saints place great importance on priesthood authority.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism:
Oneness Pentecostals baptize by immersion in the name of Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of sins, following the account in the Acts of the Apostles. They regard baptism as an essential part of the new birth, together with repentance and receiving the Holy Ghost.

They teach that the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in Jesus' command, is the single name of Jesus, and so they do not use the Trinitarian formula. Most other Protestants baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and consider Oneness teaching about God to differ from the Trinity. A Protestant reader should therefore note that Oneness Pentecostals generally rebaptize those who come from other churches, and see this as obedience, not as a judgment on earlier faith.
ortho.baptism:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, Baptism is one of the Holy Mysteries, in which a person is immersed three times in water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. It is understood as new birth, forgiveness of sins, and union with Christ in his death and resurrection.

Orthodox Christians baptize infants, and the newly baptized child is immediately chrismated, meaning anointed with holy oil to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, and given Holy Communion. There is no separation between baptism, confirmation and first communion. The Orthodox regard baptism as the beginning of a life of growth in the church. A Protestant reader should note that the whole rite is performed together, and that the Orthodox understand it as a real work of God, not a symbol only.
catholic.baptism_in_the_spirit:
In the Catholic Church, the phrase baptism in the Holy Spirit is used mainly in the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, which began in the 1960s and spread widely. Catholics involved in it understand it not as a new sacrament or a second baptism, but as a renewal or release of the grace of the Holy Spirit already given in Baptism and Confirmation.

It is often sought by prayer and the laying on of hands, and people may experience joy, a deeper faith and gifts such as tongues or prophecy. The Church has welcomed the renewal while asking that it stay in harmony with Catholic teaching. This differs from the Pentecostal teaching of a distinct experience after conversion, though the experiences often resemble each other. A Protestant reader should note the sacramental frame that Catholics keep around it.
evangelical.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Most Evangelicals teach that every believer receives the Holy Spirit at conversion, so there is no separate baptism in the Spirit that a Christian needs to seek afterwards. They point to passages saying that all believers have been baptized in one Spirit, and they emphasize being filled with the Spirit as an ongoing command, in the Letter to the Ephesians.

Being filled is understood as a continuing yielding to the Spirit's control, expressed in obedience, worship and love. Evangelicals do not generally treat speaking in tongues as the necessary sign. Some charismatic Evangelicals hold a view closer to that of Pentecostals, and others are more cautious. A Protestant reader from a Pentecostal background should note that many Evangelicals accept the gifts of the Spirit without teaching a two-stage pattern.
holiness.baptism_in_the_spirit:
In the Holiness tradition, the experience often called entire sanctification is spoken of as a second blessing: a distinct work of God's grace after conversion, in which the believer is cleansed from the inclination to sin and filled with perfect love for God and neighbor. Many Holiness writers relate it to being baptized or filled with the Holy Spirit.

Holiness churches generally do not teach that speaking in tongues is the sign of this experience. They look for its evidence in love, purity of heart and a life of holiness. Pentecostal teaching grew out of the Holiness movement and changed the emphasis to empowerment and tongues, so a Protestant reader will find the vocabulary similar but the meaning different. Holiness believers stress that the second blessing is about holiness rather than power.
lds.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Latter-day Saints speak of baptism of water and of the Spirit, following the words of Jesus to Nicodemus in the Gospel of John. After baptism in water, a person is confirmed a member of the church by the laying on of hands, and receives the gift of the Holy Ghost, which is understood as the right to the constant companionship of the Spirit if the person is faithful.

The phrase baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost is used for the sanctifying and cleansing work of the Spirit. It is not understood as a separate dramatic experience that must be sought, and speaking in tongues is treated as one gift of the Spirit among many, and not as a required sign. A Protestant reader from the Pentecostal tradition should note that the emphasis is on a gift conferred through priesthood ordinance.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spiri:
Oneness Pentecostals teach that baptism in the Holy Ghost, evidenced by speaking in tongues, is part of the new birth and is necessary for salvation, alongside repentance and baptism in the name of Jesus. They draw on the account in Acts where Peter tells the crowd to repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ and receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

Speaking in tongues is taught as the initial evidence that a person has received it. Most other Pentecostals also expect tongues, but they generally regard Spirit baptism as an experience separate from and following salvation, and not as a requirement of it. A Protestant reader should note that Oneness Pentecostals therefore treat the experience not as an addition to the Christian life but as part of what makes a person a Christian in the first place.
pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Most Pentecostals teach that baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience distinct from conversion, in which the believer is filled with the Spirit and empowered for witness and service. They base this on the accounts in the Acts of the Apostles and on the promise of Jesus that his followers would receive power.

Many Pentecostal denominations teach that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of this baptism. Believers are encouraged to seek it in prayer, and it is often received in worship services. Some Holiness Pentecostal groups describe it as a third work after conversion and sanctification. Most Evangelicals teach that the Spirit is received at conversion, and a Protestant reader should note that Pentecostals do not deny this, but hold that there is an additional filling for empowerment.
catholic.canon:
The Catholic Church holds that the Bible consists of seventy-three books: forty-six in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New Testament. The Old Testament includes the books known as deuterocanonical, such as Tobit, Wisdom and Sirach, which Protestants often call the Apocrypha.

The Church teaches that the canon was recognized by the Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, in the early centuries, and it was formally defined at the Council of Trent. Catholics point out that the early church commonly used the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which included these books. Protestants also hold that the church recognized the canon but generally follow the Hebrew Scriptures for the Old Testament, with thirty-nine books. The difference in the Old Testament list is the main difference between Catholic and Protestant Bibles.
lds.canon:
Latter-day Saints hold an open canon of scripture. Their standard works are the Bible, which in English they generally use in the King James Version, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. They regard the Book of Mormon as another testament of Jesus Christ.

They believe that God continues to reveal his will through prophets, and that the canon may therefore be added to. Statements by the church's leaders, when approved by the church, are treated as scripture in some sense. Protestants hold a closed canon of sixty-six books, and consider the canon complete. A Protestant reader should note that the phrase open canon refers to the belief that revelation and scripture can still be given, and that Latter-day Saints treat the Bible as scripture but not as the only scripture.
oriental_ortho.canon:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, do not share one uniform list of biblical books. Most include the deuterocanonical books that Protestants call the Apocrypha, in line with the early Greek Old Testament and their own ancient translations.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has an especially broad canon, which includes books such as Enoch and Jubilees that most other churches do not accept. Other Oriental Orthodox churches keep somewhat different lists. These churches regard the canon as received through the church's living tradition. A Protestant reader who expects a single closed list of sixty-six books should note that the question is not defined in the same way, and that the lists differ from one church to another.
ortho.canon:
The Eastern Orthodox Church receives the Old Testament in the form of the Greek Septuagint, which was the Bible of the early church, and so it includes books that Protestants call the Apocrypha. The Orthodox call them by the Greek word anagignoskomena, meaning things worthy to be read, and read them in worship.

The exact list of Old Testament books differs slightly among Orthodox churches, and there is no single formal decision like that of the Council of Trent for the Catholic Church. The Orthodox understand the canon as recognized within the church's tradition, and they consider that Scripture and tradition belong together. A Protestant reader will find that the New Testament is the same as in Protestant Bibles, but that the Old Testament is larger, and that the definition is less sharply drawn than in Catholic or Protestant teaching.
catholic.canonization_of_saints:
In the Catholic Church, canonization is the formal declaration by the pope, after a careful investigation, that a deceased person is in heaven and may be honored by the whole church. The process generally requires evidence of a life of heroic virtue and of miracles attributed to the person's prayers, and it normally passes through the stage of beatification.

Catholics agree with Protestants that all believers are saints in the sense of being called to holiness. They add that some people are recognized as outstanding examples and as intercessors, so that the church may be encouraged by their lives. The Church does not teach that canonization makes someone a saint, but that it acknowledges what God has done. A Protestant reader who applies the word saint to every believer will find that Catholics use the word in both senses.
ortho.canonization_of_saints:
The Eastern Orthodox Church speaks of the glorification of saints. It teaches that the church does not make a person a saint but recognizes that God has already glorified him or her. Recognition usually begins with the local veneration of a holy person by the faithful, and later a bishop or synod formally affirms it.

The process is less centralized and legalistic than in the Catholic Church, and no single authority governs it. Once a saint is glorified, a feast day is set and icons are painted. The Orthodox affirm, with Protestants, that all believers are called saints, and they also honor particular persons as friends of God who pray for the church. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox saints are venerated as part of the communion of the church, rather than worshiped.
lds.christian_status:
Whether Latter-day Saints are Christian is a question on which they and many other Christians disagree, and the disagreement is about what the word means. Latter-day Saints consider themselves Christian: they worship Jesus Christ as the Son of God and Savior, the church's official name includes his name, and they see their faith as the restoration of the church he founded.

Many other Christians, including many Protestants, hold that the Latter-day Saints stand outside historic Christianity, because they do not accept the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity, hold additional scripture, and teach a different understanding of God and of human destiny. Some Protestant bodies do not recognize Latter-day Saint baptism. Latter-day Saints reply that following Christ is what makes one Christian and that they understand the Godhead differently. Both sides use the term Christian in their own way, and it is not settled here.
catholic.church:
Catholics understand the Church as the Body of Christ, a visible community which Christ founded on the apostles, with Peter as its head, and which continues in history under the pope and the bishops in communion with him. They also speak of it as the People of God and as the sacrament of Christ's presence in the world.

Catholics teach that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, while acknowledging that many elements of truth and holiness exist in other Christian communities, whose members are united to it by Baptism. A Protestant reader may think of the church primarily as the community of all who believe in Christ, whether visible or invisible. Catholics also hold that, but they add that the Church is a visible, structured body with sacraments and a teaching authority.
lds.church:
Latter-day Saints believe that The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is the restored church of Christ, with the same organization as in the New Testament: apostles, prophets, and lay leaders serving in local congregations called wards. They call it the true and living church, because they hold that it has priesthood authority from God.

They teach that after the first century the authority and full teaching of the church were lost, and were restored in the nineteenth century through Joseph Smith. Members of other churches are regarded as sincere Christians who hold much truth and do much good, but Latter-day Saints believe that certain ordinances are valid only when performed by this authority. A Protestant reader who thinks of the church as all believers in Christ will notice that Latter-day Saints think of it as a particular organization.
ortho.church:
The Eastern Orthodox Church understands the Church as the Body of Christ, and as a communion of persons with God and with one another, centered on the Eucharist celebrated with the bishop. It confesses the Church as one, holy, catholic and apostolic, and identifies itself with that Church.

Orthodox Christians tend to think of the Church less as an institution with legal boundaries and more as a living organism in which the Holy Spirit is at work. They generally say that they know where the Church is, but do not presume to say where it is not, leaving the status of other Christians to God. A Protestant reader who thinks of the church as all believers in Christ will find that Orthodox teaching also stresses a visible communion of bishops, sacraments and councils, which it considers essential to the Church.
restorationist.church:
Restorationist Christians think of the church as the body of Christ, a people called out by God, and they look to the New Testament as the pattern for its life. Many hold that the church should be known by biblical names, such as the church of Christ or simply Christians, and should keep to biblical teaching and practice rather than later creeds and denominational traditions.

The Restorationist family is broad and its members differ on many points. Some think of many Christian communions as sharing one body, while others hold that only their own fellowship is the true church. What they share is the wish to be the New Testament church rather than a denomination. A Protestant reader will find the language of body of Christ familiar, but should note that Restorationists usually stress a particular pattern of worship and organization that they believe they are restoring.
baptist.church_and_state:
Baptists have historically been strong advocates of religious liberty and of the separation of church and state. Early Baptists, who were persecuted by established churches, argued that faith cannot be forced and that governments should not compel or prohibit worship. They spoke of soul liberty, the freedom of each person to answer to God directly.

For this reason Baptists have opposed state churches and have generally supported laws protecting freedom of conscience for everyone, including those of other faiths. The idea is rooted in the belief that the church consists of believers who have freely chosen to follow Christ. Baptists today differ on how strictly the separation should be applied in public life, and some are more open to public expressions of religion than others. A Protestant reader from an established or state church tradition will notice the difference in emphasis.
catholic.church_and_state:
Catholic teaching holds that the Church and the state are distinct communities, each with its own sphere and its own purpose: the Church concerned with salvation and moral teaching, the state with the common good of society. Each is to respect the other's proper independence and cooperate where their concerns meet.

Historically, Catholicism often had close ties with governments, and in many places was the established church. Since the Second Vatican Council the Church has taught that every person has a right to religious freedom, and that the state must not coerce belief. The Church speaks on moral questions in public life, and it offers a body of social teaching on justice and the dignity of the person. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics do not seek a theocracy, and that arrangements differ from country to country, often set out in agreements with governments.
lds.church_and_state:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints maintains that it is politically neutral. It does not endorse political parties or candidates, and does not permit its buildings or membership lists to be used for partisan purposes, although it encourages members to take part in civic life, to vote and to serve their communities.

The church sometimes speaks on public moral issues and on religious freedom, when it believes they affect the church's mission. Its Articles of Faith say that members believe in being subject to governments and in obeying and sustaining the law. Latter-day Saints also teach that the United States Constitution was established under divine inspiration. A Protestant reader will find the idea of separate spheres familiar, and should note that the church itself is highly organized and gives detailed guidance to members on many matters of life.
ortho.church_and_state:
The Eastern Orthodox tradition speaks of symphony between church and state: an ideal of harmony in which the church and the civil authority each keep their own sphere and work together for the good of the people. It grew out of the Byzantine Empire, in which the emperor and the patriarch were understood as partners, each with a distinct role.

Historically, Orthodox churches have often been closely tied to the states and nations in which they lived, sometimes protected by them and sometimes dominated. Orthodox Christians today live under many arrangements, from an established church in some countries to minority status in others, including under hostile governments. Many Orthodox themselves criticize the danger of the church becoming a tool of the state or of nationalism. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox tradition has never emphasized a strict separation in the way that Baptists do.
amish.church_discipline:
The Amish practice church discipline, including shunning, which they call Meidung. When a baptized member refuses to repent of a serious breach of the community's rules, the person is placed under the ban and the members avoid certain forms of ordinary contact, such as eating at the same table or doing business, until the person repents and makes a confession.

The purpose is not revenge. It is meant to call the person back, to protect the purity of the church and to obey what the Amish understand as the teaching of the New Testament. The same shunning applies to a baptized member who leaves the church. It is not applied to those who never joined by baptism. The strictness varies among Amish affiliations. Most Protestants practice church discipline far less formally, so a Protestant reader should note that the Amish take it very seriously as an act of love and obedience.
anabaptist.church_discipline:
Anabaptists understand the church as a community of committed believers, and they practice church discipline in the way Jesus describes in the Gospel of Matthew. A member who persists in serious sin is first spoken to privately, then with others, and finally, if there is no repentance, may be set outside the fellowship. This is called the ban.

The aim is restoration, to protect the purity of the church and to call the person back. The strictest form, shunning, is practiced most rigorously by the Amish. Many Mennonite groups practice discipline gently or seldom formally. Other Protestants also recognize church discipline, including excommunication, but many congregations rarely exercise it. A Protestant reader should note that for Anabaptists it is part of the meaning of being a baptized member, who has agreed to be accountable to the community.
catholic.church_discipline:
In the Catholic Church, the most serious penalty for grave wrongdoing is excommunication, which excludes a person from receiving the sacraments and from taking part in certain church functions. It is a medicinal penalty, meant to bring the person to repentance, and is lifted when the person repents and is reconciled.

Certain offenses, such as procuring an abortion or desecrating the Eucharist, carry excommunication automatically. The Church's canon law describes the offenses and the process. An excommunicated person remains a baptized member of the Church, with a right to return by repentance and absolution. A Protestant reader familiar with church discipline in the congregation will find that Catholic discipline is more formal, and is governed by a written body of law, as well as being applied by bishops and not by the local congregation.
lds.church_discipline:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints holds membership councils, in which a bishop or a stake president, with counselors, considers the situation of a member who has committed a serious transgression. The possible outcomes include no action, informal or formal restrictions, disfellowship, and excommunication, which ends a person's membership.

The purposes are to help the person repent, to protect the integrity of the church and to safeguard others. Councils are private, and the person concerned is invited to attend and speak. A person who has been excommunicated can be rebaptized after a period of repentance. A Protestant reader should note that this process is carried out by a single leader with counselors, and not by the congregation, and that it is a routine part of the church's life for serious matters.
catholic.clerical_celibacy:
In the Latin, or Roman, Catholic Church, priests and bishops are normally unmarried and committed to celibacy. Catholics understand this as a discipline and not a doctrine: it follows Jesus' own life and the apostle Paul's teaching that an unmarried person can give undivided attention to the Lord, and it has been the law of the Latin Church for many centuries.

Because it is a discipline and not a matter of doctrine, the Church has made exceptions. Married Protestant ministers who become Catholic may in some cases be ordained as priests, and the Eastern Catholic churches have married priests. Priests are free to serve fully without family obligations. Protestants generally allow their ministers to marry, so a Protestant reader should note that Catholics do not regard marriage as inferior, but see celibacy as a chosen gift for service.
eastern_catholic.clerical_celibacy:
In the Eastern Catholic Churches, which are in communion with the pope but keep Eastern traditions, the ordinary discipline is married clergy. A married man may be ordained a deacon and a priest, and he continues to live with his wife. A man who is already ordained may not marry, and bishops are chosen from among celibate clergy, usually monks.

This is the ancient discipline of the Eastern churches, kept when they entered communion with Rome. Practice has not been uniform everywhere. In some places, especially where Eastern Catholics live among Latin Catholics, restrictions once limited the ordination of married men, though these have been eased in recent years. A Protestant reader will find that Eastern Catholics combine Catholic teaching with the practice of married parish priests, which is the norm in most Protestant churches.
ortho.clerical_celibacy:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, parish priests and deacons may be married, but a man must marry before he is ordained, and cannot marry after ordination. If a priest's wife dies, he does not normally remarry. Bishops are chosen from among the celibate clergy, which usually means monks.

Celibacy is honored as a calling, particularly in monastic life, and Orthodox Christians do not see marriage as a lower state. The married priesthood is the ancient practice of the Eastern church and is the norm in most Orthodox parishes. A Protestant reader whose ministers are free to marry will find similarity, but should note that the timing of the marriage matters, and that bishops are almost always celibate, which affects how the church is governed.
baptist.closed_communion:
Some Baptists practice what they call close communion, meaning that the Lord's Supper is offered only to baptized believers who belong to a Baptist church, or a church of the same faith and order. The reasoning is that baptism, understood as immersion after profession of faith, comes before communion, and that communion is also a sign of agreement in doctrine.

Practice among Baptists varies widely. Many Baptist churches practice open communion, inviting all who trust in Christ, and in most Baptist bodies the decision belongs to the local church. Close communion is more common among certain traditional Baptist groups. A Protestant reader from a church that welcomes all baptized Christians should note that this is not a judgment on the faith of others, but a consequence of how Baptists connect baptism, church membership and the Supper.
catholic.closed_communion:
The Catholic Church normally offers communion only to Catholics who are properly prepared. A Catholic should be free from serious sin that has not been confessed, and should have fasted briefly beforehand. Other Christians are not usually invited to receive.

The reason is that Catholics understand receiving communion as a sign of unity in faith and in the life of the Church, so that sharing it in a divided situation would misrepresent that unity. In cases of grave necessity, a baptized Christian of another church who shares the Catholic faith in the Eucharist and who cannot reach a minister of his own church may be admitted. Catholics are also generally not to receive in Protestant churches. A Protestant reader should note that this is not meant as a judgment on their faith, and that many Catholics feel sorrow at the division it reflects.
lutheran.closed_communion:
Some Lutheran churches, including the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod, practice closed communion. Communion is offered to members of the congregation, or of churches in agreement with it in doctrine, after instruction.

The reasons given are the words of the apostle Paul about receiving the Supper worthily, the belief that receiving the Supper expresses agreement in the faith, and the pastor's responsibility for the care of those who commune. It is not intended to say that other Christians lack faith. Other Lutheran bodies, such as the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, practice a more open communion, welcoming baptized Christians from other churches. A Protestant reader from a church with open communion should note that in these Lutheran churches the Supper is understood to be the true body and blood of Christ, which is why care is taken about who receives it.
ortho.closed_communion:
The Eastern Orthodox Church normally gives communion only to Orthodox Christians who are in good standing, meaning baptized and chrismated in the Orthodox Church, and who have prepared by prayer, fasting and, usually, confession. Other Christians are welcome to attend the service but are not invited to receive.

The Orthodox understand communion as the fullest expression of unity in one faith and one church, so they do not think it right to share it where that unity does not yet exist. They regard this as a matter of honesty, and not of contempt for other Christians. It can be painful in families of mixed background. A Protestant reader from a church with an open table should note that the Orthodox hold that the Eucharist is not a fellowship meal or a means to unity, but the sign of a unity that must already exist.
catholic.communion:
Catholics call the central act of their worship the Eucharist, or the Mass. They believe that during the Mass the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, a change they call transubstantiation, and that Christ is truly present under the appearances of bread and wine. They also understand the Mass to make present Christ's one sacrifice on the cross.

Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, at least once a year and most weekly, and also adore Christ in the consecrated bread outside Mass. This differs from the Lord's Supper as most Protestants understand it, where the bread and wine are usually a memorial or a sign of Christ's spiritual presence. Catholics stress that the Mass is both a meal and a sacrifice, and that it is the source and summit of the Christian life.
anglican.confession:
Anglicans practice both a general confession, said together in every service, and a private confession to a priest. The private practice is often summarized by the saying that all may, none must, some should: it is available to anyone who wishes, but is required of no one.

The priest hears the confession under a strict seal of secrecy and pronounces God's forgiveness. It is more common among Anglo-Catholics and among some others in times of need. Many Evangelical Anglicans confess directly to God and to one another and use private confession little or not at all. A Protestant reader from a tradition that has no private confession should note that Anglicans keep it as an option, seeing it as a means of spiritual counsel and assurance and not as a required condition of forgiveness.
catholic.confession:
Catholics practice the sacrament of Reconciliation, also called Confession or Penance. A person confesses serious sins to a priest, expresses sorrow, and receives absolution, meaning the declaration of God's forgiveness, and a penance, such as prayers or acts of charity. The priest is bound by an absolute seal of secrecy.

Catholics base this on the words of Jesus in the Gospel of John giving the apostles authority to forgive and retain sins. The Church requires those aware of grave sin to confess before receiving communion, and at least once a year, and encourages more frequent use. Protestants generally confess directly to God, and sometimes to one another, holding that Christ is the only mediator. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics also believe that God alone forgives, and that the priest acts as his minister.
ortho.confession:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, Confession, also called the Mystery of Repentance, is the way a Christian confesses sins before God in the presence of a priest, who serves as witness and spiritual guide. The priest offers counsel and prays that God will forgive, and often lays a stole on the person's head during the prayer of absolution.

The emphasis falls on healing rather than on legal judgment. Sin is understood as a sickness, and the priest as a physician who helps the person to change. Orthodox Christians normally confess regularly, especially before receiving communion, and often to a spiritual father whom they know well. A Protestant reader who confesses directly to God will find that the Orthodox also emphasize confession to God, but hold that it is good to make it before a priest, as a witness in the church.
anglican.confirmation:
In Anglican churches, confirmation is the rite in which a baptized person, guided by the bishop, publicly reaffirms the promises made at baptism and receives the bishop's prayer and the laying on of hands for the strengthening of the Holy Spirit. It is normally for those who are old enough to make their own profession of faith.

Anglican teaching names Baptism and the Lord's Supper as the two sacraments given by Christ in the gospel, and confirmation is not one of them, though Anglo-Catholics count it among seven. In earlier times it was required before receiving communion, but many Anglican provinces now admit baptized children to communion first. A Protestant reader from a church that baptizes infants and later holds a rite of profession will recognize a similar pattern, and should note that Anglican confirmation is done by a bishop.
catholic.confirmation:
In the Catholic Church, Confirmation is a sacrament of Christian initiation, together with Baptism and the Eucharist. The bishop, or a priest he authorizes, anoints the person with blessed oil called chrism on the forehead, lays hands on him or her, and prays for the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Catholics understand it as completing the grace of Baptism, strengthening the believer to live and to witness to the faith. It is received once and cannot be repeated, and in the Latin Church it is usually received in the teenage years, though the age varies, and adults who enter the Church receive it with their Baptism. Many Protestants have a rite of confirmation as a public profession of faith. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics treat it not only as a personal profession but as a sacrament in which grace is conferred.
lutheran.confirmation:
In Lutheran churches confirmation is not regarded as a sacrament. It is a rite that follows a period of instruction in the faith, usually based on Luther's Small Catechism, at which baptized young people publicly affirm the faith into which they were baptized and, in many churches, are admitted to receive the Lord's Supper.

The rite marks the completion of a period of basic teaching and does not add anything to Baptism. The age and the way it is done vary by church and region, and some churches admit younger children to communion before confirmation. A Protestant reader will find this familiar, since many Protestant churches have a similar rite. Lutherans stress that it is a public affirmation of a faith which God has already given in Baptism, and not the moment at which a person becomes a Christian.
oriental_ortho.confirmation:
In the Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, the rite corresponding to confirmation is called chrismation. The newly baptized person is anointed with holy oil, often called myron, which has been consecrated by the church's senior bishops, and this anointing is understood as the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.

It is performed immediately after baptism, including for infants, and is followed by Holy Communion, so that baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist form one act of initiation. There is no later rite of confirmation. A Protestant reader from a church where confirmation comes years after baptism as a personal profession should note that in these churches the gift of the Spirit is given at the outset of Christian life, and personal commitment is expected to grow within the church's life afterwards.
ortho.confirmation:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, Chrismation is the rite that corresponds to confirmation, and it takes place immediately after Baptism. The priest anoints the newly baptized person with holy oil, called myron, that has been consecrated by a bishop, touching the forehead, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, chest, hands and feet, and saying: The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Infants are chrismated at the same service as their baptism and then receive Holy Communion. Orthodox teaching understands this as personal Pentecost, the bestowal of the Holy Spirit on the new Christian. Converts from other Christian churches are sometimes received by chrismation alone. A Protestant reader accustomed to confirmation as a later public profession of faith should note that in Orthodoxy the whole process of Christian initiation is done together, and profession is expected to grow through a lifetime.
catholic.continuationism:
Catholics teach that the Holy Spirit continues to give gifts, called charisms, to members of the Church, as described in the First Letter to the Corinthians. These can include gifts of healing, prophecy, tongues and others, and they are understood as given for the good of the Church and to be discerned by its pastors.

The Catholic Church does not hold that the miraculous gifts ended with the apostles. Miracles are reported in the lives of saints and at pilgrimage sites, and the Catholic Charismatic Renewal has emphasized the gifts since the 1960s. The Church investigates claimed miracles carefully. It teaches that no gift adds to the revelation given in Christ. A Protestant reader from a tradition that holds the sign gifts have ceased will find that Catholics are broadly continuationist, while keeping the gifts under the authority of the Church.
evangelical.continuationism:
Evangelicals are divided on whether the sign gifts of the New Testament, such as tongues, prophecy and healing, continue today. Some, called cessationists, teach that these gifts ended with the apostolic age. Others, called continuationists, believe they are still given. Many are somewhere in between, described as open but cautious.

The disagreement is sometimes called the charismatic question, and it does not usually divide Evangelicals over the essentials of the gospel. Both sides hold that Scripture is complete and sufficient. Baptist and Reformed Evangelicals more often lean toward cessationism, while Evangelicals from charismatic and Pentecostal backgrounds affirm the gifts. A Protestant reader will find that Evangelicals have no single position here, and that congregations differ widely in how they treat the gifts in worship.
pentecostal.continuationism:
Pentecostals teach continuationism: the spiritual gifts and signs of the New Testament, including healing, prophecy and tongues, have not ceased and remain available to the church today. They find no statement in Scripture that these gifts would end before Christ returns, and they read the passage about gifts passing away as referring to his return.

They also point to the testimony of believers around the world who report experiences of the Spirit's power. They hold that the gifts are to be tested against Scripture, and that Scripture remains the final authority. Protestants who teach that the sign gifts ceased with the apostolic age, called cessationists, understand the same passages differently. A Protestant reader will find that Pentecostals see this difference as one of the most important between themselves and other churches.
reformed.continuationism:
The traditional Reformed view is cessationism: the extraordinary gifts of the apostolic age, such as new revelation, apostolic miracles and tongues, ceased when the foundation of the church was laid and Scripture was completed. The Westminster Confession says that the earlier ways of God's revealing his will have now ceased, because Scripture is complete.

This does not mean that Reformed Christians think God has stopped acting. They pray for healing, believe God answers prayer, and affirm his providence in all things.
