What they deny is that sign gifts such as tongues and prophecy continue as ordinary features of church life. Some Reformed teachers today are open to them, provided they never rival Scripture. A Protestant reader from a Pentecostal or charismatic background will find that the Reformed stress the completeness of Scripture as the reason.
reformed_baptist.continuationism:
Reformed Baptists commonly hold to cessationism: the view that the miraculous sign gifts of the apostolic age, such as speaking in tongues and apostolic healings, served to confirm the message of the apostles and ceased when that foundational period ended. Scripture is regarded as complete and sufficient, so God no longer gives new revelation through prophecy.

This does not mean that Reformed Baptists think God has stopped acting. They pray for the sick, believe God answers prayer, and affirm his providential care. The difference concerns whether the sign gifts continue as ordinary features of church life. Not every Reformed Baptist holds the cessationist view with the same strength, and some describe themselves as open but cautious. A Protestant reader should note that this is the historic stance of Calvinistic Baptists and is grounded in the sufficiency of Scripture.
catholic.continuing_revelation:
The Catholic Church teaches that public revelation, the revelation given for the whole Church, was completed with Christ and the apostles, and that it ended with the death of the last apostle. The Church does not expect any new public revelation to be added to Scripture and Tradition, though it believes its understanding of that revelation can deepen over time.

Catholics do acknowledge private revelations, such as the apparitions at Lourdes and Fatima, which the Church may examine and approve as worthy of belief. Even when approved, these are not obligatory for Catholics, and they cannot add to the deposit of faith. A Protestant reader who holds to the sufficiency of Scripture will find that Catholics also regard revelation as closed, though they place Tradition and the Church's teaching alongside Scripture in guarding it.
lds.continuing_revelation:
Latter-day Saints believe that God continues to reveal his will today through living prophets, as he did in Bible times. They sustain the president of the church as a prophet, seer and revelator, together with the apostles, and they believe these leaders receive revelation for the church as a whole.

Latter-day Saints also teach that every person can receive personal revelation, for their own life and responsibilities, through the Holy Ghost. They hold that revelation never contradicts what God has revealed before. It is one reason why they accept additional scripture beyond the Bible. Most Protestants teach that Scripture is sufficient and that revelation is closed with the New Testament. A Protestant reader should therefore see that the phrase continuing revelation, for Latter-day Saints, describes a central way in which they believe the church is guided.
new_apostolic.continuing_revelation:
The New Apostolic Church teaches that Jesus Christ has continued to send apostles to his church, just as he did in the New Testament, and that this continuing apostleship is the way he guides and builds up his people today. The apostles preach the gospel, teach, and care for the unity of the church, and the church is led by a Chief Apostle.

Members do not understand this as adding new books to Scripture. The Bible remains the foundation, and the apostles' role is to interpret and apply it, and to lead the church in obedience to Christ. A Protestant reader who holds that the apostolic age ended in the first century should note that the New Apostolic Church regards the apostolic office, and the guidance that comes through it, as continuing, though it does not claim to add to the canon.
pentecostal.continuing_revelation:
Pentecostals believe in prophecy as a gift of the Holy Spirit that continues in the church today. In their understanding, prophecy is a word from God given through a believer to encourage, strengthen and comfort others, as described in the First Letter to the Corinthians, and God may also guide individuals by the Spirit.

They do not understand such words as adding to Scripture. The Bible is complete and is the standard by which every prophetic word is tested, and the congregation or its leaders are expected to weigh what is said. A prophecy that contradicts Scripture is rejected. Many Protestants hold to the sufficiency of Scripture and teach that God no longer speaks through prophecy. A Protestant reader should note that Pentecostals agree that Scripture is final, but believe that God still speaks within its limits.
seventh_day_adventist.continuing_revelat:
Seventh-day Adventists believe that the gift of prophecy, which is listed among the gifts of the Spirit in the New Testament, continues in the church. They understand it as having been manifested in the ministry of Ellen G. White, who was a leader in the early Adventist movement in the nineteenth century, and they refer to her writings as the Spirit of Prophecy.

Adventists hold that her writings provide guidance, encouragement and correction, but they do not treat them as a replacement for the Bible. Scripture remains the standard by which all teaching, including hers, is tested. The Bible is the final authority. A Protestant reader who holds that the sufficiency of Scripture excludes any continuing prophetic gift should note that Adventists see her writings as subordinate to Scripture and not as an addition to it.
